mathprize-olympiad-2025-01.title: Repeating 2025
mathprize-olympiad-2025-01.body:
**Yes.** For $r\ge1$ let $N_r$ be the number whose decimal expansion is $2025$ written $r$ times, i.e. $N_r=2025\,(1+10^4+10^8+\dots+10^{4(r-1)})$.

Then $N_r$ ends in the digit $5$, so it is not divisible by $10$. Since $2025=9\cdot225$,
$$\frac{N_r}9=225\,(1+10^4+\dots+10^{4(r-1)}),$$
whose decimal expansion is $225$ followed by $r-1$ blocks $0225$, i.e. $225\,0225\,0225\cdots0225$.

Digit counts: $N_r$ has $r$ zeros, $2r$ twos and $r$ fives. $N_r/9$ has $r-1$ zeros, $2+2(r-1)=2r$ twos and $1+(r-1)=r$ fives. So $N_r/9$ is exactly $N_r$ with one digit $0$ erased and the remaining digits reordered, and $9\cdot\frac{N_r}9=N_r$. Hence every $N_r$ is amazing, giving infinitely many amazing numbers not divisible by $10$. (For $r=1$: erasing the $0$ of $2025$ gives $225$, and $9\cdot225=2025$.) ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2025-02.title: Double counting edges
mathprize-olympiad-2025-02.body:
Suppose, for contradiction, that every edge joins a vertex of odd degree to a vertex of even degree. Then every edge has exactly one endpoint of even degree, so counting each edge at its even-degree endpoint,
$$\#\text{edges}=\sum_{v:\ \deg v\text{ even}}\deg v,$$
which is a sum of even numbers, hence even. But a tree on $n$ vertices has $n-1$ edges, which is odd since $n$ is even. Contradiction. So some edge joins two vertices whose degrees have the same parity. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2025-03.title: Complex numbers: few possible final points
mathprize-olympiad-2025-03.body:
**Hannah wins.**

Take $\Gamma$ as the unit circle in $\mathbb C$. For points $a\ne b$ on it, $\dfrac{a-b}{\overline a-\overline b}=\dfrac{a-b}{(b-a)/(ab)}=-ab$, so the chord $AB$ has direction $e^{i\theta}$ with $e^{2i\theta}=-ab$. Chords $AB$ and $PQ$ are perpendicular iff their directions differ by $90^\circ$, i.e. $e^{2i\theta_{AB}}=-e^{2i\theta_{PQ}}$, i.e. $-ab=-(-pq)$, so $ab=-pq$. Thus an operation replaces $(a,b,p)$ by
$$q=-\frac{ab}{p}.$$

**Claim.** If a sequence of operations combines $2k+1$ points $z_1,\dots,z_{2k+1}$ of $S$ into a single point, that point equals
$$(-1)^k\frac{\text{product of some }k+1\text{ of the }z_i}{\text{product of the other }k}.$$
*Proof* by induction on $k$ ($k=0$: the point itself). The last operation combines three points $c_1,c_2,c_3$ that were obtained from groups of $2k_1+1,2k_2+1,2k_3+1$ original points with $k_1+k_2+k_3+1=k$. By induction $c_j=(-1)^{k_j}N_j/D_j$ with $N_j$ a product of $k_j+1$ of the points of its group and $D_j$ a product of the other $k_j$. The result is
$$-\frac{c_1c_2}{c_3}=(-1)^{1+k_1+k_2+k_3}\frac{N_1N_2D_3}{D_1D_2N_3}=(-1)^k\frac{N_1N_2D_3}{D_1D_2N_3},$$
where the numerator has $(k_1+1)+(k_2+1)+k_3=k+1$ factors and the denominator $k_1+k_2+k_3+1=k$ factors. $\square$

**Application.** Each operation reduces $|S|$ by $2$, and every original point not yet used remains in $S$; to end with a single point from $13$ points, all $13$ original points are combined into it (so $k=6$). By the claim the final point is $\dfrac{\text{product of 7 of the original points}}{\text{product of the other 6}}$, which is determined by which $6$ of the $13$ original points go in the denominator. So Jessica can only end at one of at most $\binom{13}6=1716<2025$ points.

Hannah, who sees $S$, chooses $T$ to contain all these (at most) $1716$ candidate points, padded to $2025$ points with arbitrary other points of $\Gamma$. Then whatever Jessica does, a final single point lies in $T$, and Jessica never wins. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2025-04.title: Cyclic quadrilateral and reflection
mathprize-olympiad-2025-04.body:
Let $p=\angle QPR$, $q=\angle PQR$, $r=\angle PRQ$ (all $<90^\circ$), $\alpha=\angle BQP=\angle BPQ$ (as $BP=BQ$) and $\beta=\angle CPR=\angle CRP$ (as $CP=CR$).

**Angle at $A$.** At $P$, on line $BC$: $\alpha+p+\beta=180^\circ$. At $Q$ on $AB$: $\angle AQR=180^\circ-\alpha-q$; at $R$ on $AC$: $\angle ARQ=180^\circ-\beta-r$. So in triangle $AQR$,
$$\angle QAR=180^\circ-\angle AQR-\angle ARQ=\alpha+\beta+q+r-180^\circ=(180^\circ-p)+(180^\circ-p)-180^\circ=180^\circ-2p.$$

**Angle at $D$.** Tangents at $Q,R$ meet at $D$ with $DQ=DR$ and $\angle QDR=180^\circ-\angle QOR=180^\circ-2p$ ($O$ the circumcentre of $PQR$; the angle $QPR=p$ is acute so $\angle QOR=2p$). The point $D$ lies on the opposite side of $QR$ from $P$ (the centre $O$ is on $P$'s side since $p<90^\circ$). The point $A$ also lies on the opposite side of line $QR$ from $P$ (line $QR$ separates $A$ from $B$, $C$, and hence from $P\in BC$).

**$D$ lies on the external bisector.** $A$ and $D$ lie on the same side of $QR$ and both see $QR$ under the angle $180^\circ-2p$, so $A,D,Q,R$ are concyclic (or $A=D$). Since $DQ=DR$, $D$ is the midpoint of the arc $QR$ of this circle containing $A$, and the line $AD$ is therefore the external angle bisector of $\angle QAR$, which is the external bisector $\ell$ of $\angle BAC$ ($Q\in AB$, $R\in AC$). (If $A=D$ then $D\in\ell$ trivially.)

**Reflection.** Reflect $C$ in $\ell$ to $C'$. Because $\ell$ is the external bisector, $C'$ lies on line $AB$ on the other side of $A$ from $B$, with $AC'=AC$. As $D\in\ell$, $DC'=DC$, so
$$DB+DC=DB+DC'\ge BC'=BA+AC'=AB+AC.\ ∎$$
